claims.claim: Passwords remain a widely used form of authentication despite well-known usability and security concerns, which is why they are still a prime target of attackers.
Short passwords are weak because they yield to brute-force and dictionary attacks; NIST names password length a primary factor in password strength.
Simple, common passwords (such as '12345') and passwords built from personal facts (such as birthdays and pet names) are not safe for protecting accounts that hold personal information.

Current guidance puts length ahead of complexity: NIST directs verifiers not to impose composition rules (forced mixtures of character types) on passwords, and CISA recommends passwords of at least 16 characters, longer is stronger.
A passphrase — a password made of a sequence of words, ideally four to seven unrelated words with spaces allowed — is an effective way to create a longer, stronger password.
Users should not be forced to change passwords periodically; a forced change is appropriate only on evidence of compromise, such as a breach or suspected leak.

Reusing a password across accounts is the biggest multiplier of damage: a password leaked from one service can be tried against the user's other accounts (password stuffing), turning one breach into many.

Password managers generate, store, and fill in unique strong passwords per account, so the user memorizes only one strong master password; NIST requires verifiers to allow password-manager use and autofill.

No password is unbreakable: attacks such as keystroke logging, phishing, and social engineering capture the password regardless of its length or complexity, so a password is one layer of a layered defense, with multi-factor authentication as the next layer.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How often users should change their passwords
positions: Long-standing enterprise practice forced periodic password changes (for example every 60-90 days).

Current NIST SP 800-63B guidance states verifiers shall not require subscribers to change passwords periodically; a change is forced only on evidence of compromise. OWASP's Authentication Cheat Sheet repeats this position, citing NIST.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the current guidance: change a password when there is evidence it was compromised, not on a calendar schedule, and explains why scheduled changes produce predictable, weaker passwords.

conflictingEvidence.issue: What makes a password strong: complexity versus length
positions: Older policies required composition rules — forced mixtures of character types such as uppercase letters, digits, and symbols.

NIST SP 800-63B states length is a primary factor in password strength, directs verifiers not to impose composition rules, and notes passphrases as an effective way to gain length. CISA's consumer guidance recommends at least 16 characters and passphrases of 4-7 unrelated words.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson teaches the length-first guidance and attributes it to NIST and CISA, noting that complexity rules remain permitted but are no longer the main lever.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated phase-2 draft for this topic contained only generic boilerplate ('Password Security is a foundational concept in Cybersecurity', generic objectives about defining and applying the concept) with no specific factual claims; no draft claims were retained.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the generic draft boilerplate with sourced content on password weakness factors, length-first guidance, no-forced-rotation guidance, reuse risk, and password managers.
Corrected the implicit complexity-first framing of older guidance with the current length-first position, attributed to NIST SP 800-63B (fourth revision) and CISA Secure Our World.
Added the honest-framing claim that no password is unbreakable and that defense is layered, with MFA referenced as the sibling-topic safety net.

sourceRecords.title: NIST Special Publication 800-63B: Authentication and Authenticator Management
sourceRecords.provider: National Institute of Standards and Technology
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at pages.nist.gov (SP 800-63B, fourth revision) on 2026-08-21. Supports: passwords as a widely used form of authentication; length as a primary factor in password strength; short passwords yielding to brute-force and dictionary attacks; minimum lengths (15 characters when the password is the only authentication factor, at least 8 when used within MFA); verifiers SHALL NOT impose composition rules or require periodic password changes, with forced change only on evidence of compromise; passphrases as an effective way to create longer passwords; distinct passwords as protection against password stuffing (a compromised password from one site used to access the user's accounts on other sites); verifiers SHALL allow password managers and autofill, with password generators leading to stronger passwords; and the observation that keystroke logging, phishing, and social engineering are not defeated by password complexity or length. Facts synthesized into original lesson prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Use Strong Passwords (Secure Our World)
sourceRecords.notes: U.S. federal government consumer guidance (public domain). The live host blocks automated fetchers (HTTP 403), so the page was read via the Wayback Machine snapshot of 2026-06-03 (web.archive.org/web/20260603221105/), where it carries an 'Archived Content' banner noting it may not reflect current policy; the guidance content matches the current NIST position. Supports: strong passwords are long (at least 16 characters, longer is stronger), random (a random string or a memorable passphrase of 4-7 unrelated words, spaces allowed), and unique (a different password for every account); simple passwords such as '12345' and common identifying information like birthdays and pet names are not safe; weak passwords can be quickly broken by computer hackers; the 'Emma' case in which one reused password turned a company breach into bank and email account takeover; password managers generate, store, and fill in passwords so the user remembers only one strong master password; and MFA as an additional layer of protection. Facts synthesized into original lesson prose; no wording reproduced.

sourceRecords.title: Authentication Cheat Sheet
sourceRecords.notes: Read live at cheatsheetseries.owasp.org on 2026-08-21. Used for corroboration of two points only: minimum password length as the defining attribute of a strong password (with the NIST-derived thresholds of 8 characters when MFA is enabled and 15 when it is not), and the statement that verifiers should not mandate arbitrary periodic password changes, per NIST guidelines. The lesson cites it alongside NIST; all prose is original synthesis.
